(Xinhua/Yao Dawei) BEIJING, July 23 (Xinhua) -- Wang Huning, chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), met with Tomio Okamura, speaker of the Chamber of Deputies of the Czech Republic, in Beijing on Thursday. Noting that the friendly communication between the people of China and the Czech Republic has a long history, Wang said that the two countries share huge potential and broad prospects for bilateral cooperation. China is willing to join hands with the Czech side to strengthen practical cooperation and promote the traditional friendship to regain vitality, while respecting each other's core interests and major concerns, he said. Wang introduced China's positions on issues related to Taiwan and Xizang, saying that the CPPCC National Committee stands ready to contribute to promoting the healthy and stable development of China-Czech relations. Okamura said that the Czech Republic adheres to the one-China policy, and the Czech side is willing to take the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the strategic partnership between the two countries as an opportunity to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with China, and promote the development of bilateral relations. The Chamber of Deputies is willing to play an active role in promoting collaboration in various areas between the two countries and enhancing friendship between the two peoples, said Okamura. The operation of Units 1 and 2 of Cernavoda NPP is carried out based on strict monitoring of operating parameters and safety margins, as well as on procedures specific to drought conditions; thus, as long as the analysis of these parameters allows the operation in compliance with all nuclear safety norms, Unit 2 will remain connected to the National Energy System. Key parameters remained stable overnight, and, at this time, the necessary conditions are in place to temporarily continue the operation of Unit 2. Nuclearelectrica is making every possible effort to continue operations under conditions of maximum safety and to contribute to the stability of the National Energy System, continuously analyzing and monitoring all parameters that could drop to minimum levels without affecting the safe operation of the facilities. Given both the current situation and the hydrological forecasts regarding the Danube’s water level, the shutdown of Unit 2 may be necessary at any time, depending heavily on any adverse fluctuations that occur and their effects on the plant’s systems. Nuclearelectrica will inform subsequently. Unit 1 of the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant remains safely shut down until the Danube’s water level allows the safe reconnection to the National Energy System (NES). https://www.thelocal.de/20260812/today-i.text: Advertisement Today in Germany Members only Today in Germany: A roundup of the latest news on Wednesday Rachel Loxton - rachel.loxton@thelocal.com Published: 12 Aug, 2026 CET. Updated: Wed 12 Aug 2026 08:29 CET Share Add a comment Stacks of solar eclipse viewing glasses displayed at a store in Paris on August 11, 2026, on the eve of a partial solar eclipse. (Photo by Lou BENOIST / AFP) Flight delays at Hanover Airport after drone sighting, Germany prepares for partial solar eclipse, climate activists deflate SUV tires on Sylt and more news from Germany this Wednesday, August 12th. Wednesday's top story: Hanover Airport disrupted by drone week after Leipzig explosives find Hanover Airport in Germany was disrupted overnight by a drone, police said on Tuesday without giving further details, just a week after an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport. "The investigation into the drone overflight at Langenhagen Airport on Tuesday has been taken over by the Hanover Central Criminal Investigation Department," a local police spokeswoman told AFP. Runways at the airport, located north of Hanover, were closed for 90 minutes early Tuesday morning before normal operations resumed, an airport spokeswoman told AFP. Six flights – including departures to Turkey, Egypt, Greece, and Spain – were delayed by 15 to 50 minutes, according to the spokeswoman. A cargo plane from Paris was also diverted to Nuremberg Airport. Germany prepares for partial solar eclipse Tonight is the night! In the lead up to sunset, people in Germany will be able to witness the most impressive solar eclipse ( Sonnenfinsternis or SoFi ) in decades. While some countries will see a full eclipse, the moon will block between 80 and 90 percent of the sun's light depending on where you are in Germany. The eclipse begins between roughly 7:10pm and 7:25pm, depending on your location. It will reach its maximum shortly after 8pm in Germany and continue until sunset, with northern parts of the country enjoying slightly longer viewing times. Don't forget that you need special eclipse glasses, certified to the DIN EN ISO 12312-2:2015 standard, to look at the sun. Advertisement Retailers in Germany have been running low on stocks. Readers told The Local that the Planetarium Berlin has been giving out eclipse glasses. Following the eclipse, observers may be able to see a collection of shooting stars as August 12th marks the peak of the Perseid meteor shower. READ ALSO: What to do if you can't find eclipse glasses in Germany How to view the solar eclipse from Germany on August 12th German power prices to briefly surge during eclipse Speaking of the eclipse, electricity prices in Germany are set to briefly surge during the event, highlighting the country's growing dependence on the power of the sun. Spot electricity for Wednesday evening – when a partial solar eclipse will largely block out the sun – was selling for some 15-minute periods at over €400 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), more than double Tuesday's price at the same time, according to European Power Exchange data. Prices for the period between 7:45pm and 8pm on Wednesday – around the peak of the eclipse – were selling for as much as €461.17. Wholesale prices on the exchange are set a day in advance for each 15-minute period through auctions between power producers and large consumers. Such sharp fluctuations are common in a German market increasingly shaped by renewable energy, the supply of which can be intermittent and depend on the weather. Advertisement BSW backs working with AfD following the state election in Saxony-Anhalt The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) has spoken out in favour of involving the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in government following the state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The move would break a long-held firewall that political parties in Germany have against associating with the far-right party. The AfD is leading the polls with around 42 percent, followed by the CDU (22 percent), and Die Linke or The Left (13 percent). "Our aim is to oust the incumbent CDU state premier" co-chair Amira Mohamed Ali told German newspaper the Rheinische Post. The BSW wants to see a cross-party state premier who governs with shifting majorities "including the AfD". "Regardless of one’s views on this party’s positions, if they receive around 40 percent of the vote, they cannot be completely ignored," said Mohamed Ali. The AfD’s campaign platform for Saxony-Anhalt includes pushing a "deportation offensive", forcing integration courses on foreign residents and limiting religious freedoms. The election or Landtagswahl takes place on September 6th. READ ALSO: Election guide - Germany's main political parties explained Ulrich Siegmund, AfD top candidate for Saxony-Anhalt, addresses supporters during an election campaign event ahead of the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, in Magdeburg, eastern Germany on July 18, 2026. Slogan reads "Everything is possible". (Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP) Climate activists deflate SUV tires on Sylt Climate activists deflated the tires of numerous cars on Tuesday on the North Sea island of Sylt. A group referring to itself as a 'resistance collective' claimed in an email that it had "deflated about 50 luxury cars". Local police spoke said they knew of around 20 cases by noon. "The investigations have been started," a police spokeswoman told DPA. However, the act was "not a criminal offence", police noted, because the tyres were not destroyed. Rather than slashing the tyres, the activists had let out their air. A message from the resistance group was left on affected vehicles, which said that the action was not personal but taken against "expensive cars" and their environmental impacts. Similar incidents have previously been reported in Germany and elsewhere in Europe, usually undertaken by an anonymous and loosely organised group which calls itself 'The Tyre Extinguishers'. READ ALSO: Why an anonymous group has been deflating tyres of SUVs across Germany German prosecutors drop probe into navy sabotage suspects An investigation into two men suspected of attempting to sabotage German naval vessels last year has been stopped for lack of evidence, prosecutors said Tuesday. The two men, a 37-year-old Romanian and a 54-year-old Greek, were arrested in February on suspicion of acts of sabotage targeting vessels to be delivered to the German navy. Advertisement The men, who worked at the Hamburg port at the time, were accused of putting more than 20 kilogrammes (about 40 pounds) of grit into one ship's engine block, puncturing water supply lines, removing caps from fuel tanks and deactivating electronic safety switches. The attempted sabotage was discovered in time to avoid any further damage. The suspects were freed from detention in March while the investigation continued. But prosecutors told AFP on Tuesday that "proceedings against both suspects have been discontinued". They added that they are "convinced that the corvettes were tampered with, in particular through cutting off the electricity on the 'Koeln'", one of the ships. Prosecutors said "it could not be established which of the two suspects carried out the alleged activity with the degree of certainty needed to file charges". Nor could it be proven that two acted as "co-conspirators on the basis of a joint plan", they added. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian Nepal-Tibet flood disaster ‘The river has taken everything’: people return to remains of their homes in Nepal Precariousness of living in Devighat by the Trishuli River underlined as waters swell again and residents flee to higher ground Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Devighat Sun 30 Aug 2026 12.39 EDT Last modified on Sun 30 Aug 2026 16.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The bodies continue to wash up. But the morgues have already run out of room. Since the deadly floods coursed through the Himalayan valleys of Nepal and Tibet, the numbers of people killed have continued to rise. The bodies have surfaced in their hundreds and continue to be pulled from the thick, tar-like mud that engulfed everything after the flood waters receded. By Sunday, the death toll stood at 797 in Nepal and Tibet. Morgues across Nepal are already overflowing. Authorities say they are overwhelmed with the task of trying to identify the dead, many mangled beyond recognition and turning up miles from home. As places to safely store the victims run out, mass burials have begun in the district of Bharatpur. Satellite image of Nepal showing location of Devighat DNA samples were taken from each body before it was given a tag and a location number, wrapped in a plastic bag and then placed in a shallow grave. The hope, said the police, was that these bodies would eventually be identified by loved ones through DNA and retrieved for proper funeral rites. In Chitwan, about 100 miles downstream from the region worst hit by the flash floods and mudslides, more than 250 bodies have washed up along the riverbanks. But they are in such a disfigured state that only nine have been successfully identified. Many will now be buried, at least temporarily, in the forest on the edge of the city. Residents try to salvage belongings from their damaged homes In an effort to speed up the identification exercise, local officials have adopted a macabre approach of simply asking people to go through pictures of the bodies and look for identifying features: a necklace, a wedding ring, a tattoo, a scar. Photos of those recovered have been placed on to PowerPoint slideshows, for relatives to sit patiently through, and have been uploaded to the Nepal police website. Outside the morgue in the capital, Kathmandu, photographs of the dead inside have been posted on the walls. Yet with more than 3,000 still reported missing in Nepal and Tibet, there are fears that the numbers of dead may still rise exponentially. Many of the worst-hit areas, where entire villages were wiped away by the tidal wave of mud, water and debris, are still inaccessible except by army helicopter. Speaking on Sunday, the foreign secretary, Amrit Bahadur Rai, said the Nepal government had requested “more than 1,000 freezer units” for safe storage of the dead. View image in fullscreen People searching for their belongings in their mud-damaged home in Devighat. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian Even in areas lower down the river valley that were decimated by the floods but have remained accessible by road, search and rescue teams have struggled to retrieve all those killed and buried in the mud. On Sunday afternoon in Devighat, a sacred town on the Trishuli River that was left in ruins by the floods, police search and rescue teams prepared to pull another victim from the muddy ruins of a house. All that was visible through the thick mud was their feet. “It is very tough work. We have retrieved 10 bodies from here so far, maybe there will be more,” said Amabadutta Bhatta, a police superintendent working as part of search and rescue in the city. “The floods destroyed the first and second storey of most homes here. When we finally clear all the mud, which may be many months, who knows what we might find.” Nepal-Tibet deaths from flash flooding rise amid race to free workers in tunnel Read more Those who survived the floods in Devighat have slowly come back to see the remains of their houses, many of which were wiped away altogether. Standing next to the carcass of her house, reduced to a few concrete blocks and twisted metal, Usha Nepali, 49, wept for the home where she had raised her four children and then her three grandchildren. View image in fullscreen People in Devighat salvage what possessions they can from their damaged homes. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian “I invested everything to build this house, so now I don’t know where to go and what to do,” said Nepali. “Nothing is left except this cloth on my back. I haven’t even been able to change clothes since the floods. How can we rebuild this house? This land is no longer safe but it’s the only land we have. The river has taken everything.” The precariousness of living next to the Trishuli River was underlined on Sunday as the fast-moving waters again swelled dangerously high and rescuers urged people to get to higher ground quickly. Many in Devighat were packing up the few items they could find in their homes, never to return. Jamuna Magar, 36, said her husband’s family had been living in Devighat for generations. She had come here when she got married and described it as “such a beautiful place”. View image in fullscreen Many returned to Devighat to pack up their belongings before leaving, never to return. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian In the minutes after they got warning of the flood, she had time to grab her gold but nothing else. As she stood by the ruins of her house, clutching the only thing she had been able to retrieve so far – a plastic vat of vegetable cooking oil – she said she did not see how they could ever live in Devighat again. “We had experienced flooding before, but we never knew a flood like this could come and take our house,” she said. “Everything we owned was on the ground floor of the house and now it’s all lost. Even our refrigerator washed away. I’m too worried about my life, about my children’s lives to stay here any longer.” She feared it would take “decades before they can rebuild Devighat again”. https://www.dw.com/en/us-congress-passes.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MjJY The bill was passed by 262-159, after breezing through the Senate last month in an 86-11 vote [FILE: Feb 5, 2019] Image: Alex Edelman/CNP/picture alliance Advertisement The US Republican-led US House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine. The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month. The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it. Russia's economy is growing, despite sanctions To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What does the sanctions package against Russia entail? The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet , old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions. More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries that rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures. The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran. It was drafted in April 2025 by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July . But Trump had delayed the bill's passage, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress. How much leverage does the US have over its adversaries? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Who opposed the bill and why? Democrats who voted for the bill broke ranks with the party leadership, which argues the legislation expands Trump's tariff powers and that the president already has the power to sanction Russia should he choose to. "What this legislation will do ​is give Donald Trump, perhaps, unfettered authority to unleash ⁠tariffs on the American people," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a speech on Wednesday. Meanwhile, some Republicans opposed to the bill were wary of compounded tariffs further increasing consumer prices ahead of the midterm elections in November. The bill's supporters say it is integral to keeping up the pressure on Russia. It has been celebrated by Ukrainian activists. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with lawmakers to urge its passage and even watched an early procedural vote from the chamber. https://www.geosuper.tv/latest/59347-dam.text: Boxing Damian Knyba defeats Andy Ruiz Jr in comeback bout Knyba improves professional record to 18-1 By Web Desk September 05, 2026 An undated picture of Andy Ruiz Jr. — X/ @andy_destroyer1 Andy Ruiz Jr lost his comeback bout against Poland’s Damian Knyba by unanimous decision, with the judges scoring the fight 117-110, 114-113 and 114-113 in favour of Knyba here at the Prudential Center on Friday. The 36-year-old former world heavyweight champion was fighting for only the fourth time since losing his rematch against Britain’s Anthony Joshua in December 2019. Ruiz Jr struggled to find his rhythm throughout the fight and was knocked down in the seventh round. ANDY RUIZ IS SAVED BY THE BELL 🤯🤯🤯 #TheFight | #RuizKnyba | Live NOW on DAZN and TNT ▪️ pic.twitter.com/JVQjG3KQM3 — DAZN Boxing (@DAZNBoxing) September 5, 2026 He managed to beat the count but was unable to turn the bout around as Knyba secured the biggest win of his career. Despite the defeat, Ruiz Jr said he wants an immediate rematch and believes he can perform much better next time. "I don't know, I think it was just him holding," said Ruiz Jr, who recently signed with British promoter Eddie Hearn. "Every time I tried to come in, he'd hold me really tight, and I just couldn't let my combinations go. "He played a good game plan, but I'd love to run it back and do things a lot different." Ruiz Jr also blamed his performance on a long period away from the ring. His previous fight was a draw against American Jarrell Miller in August 2024. "It was just a long layoff, and it was a great opponent," he said. "I didn't want to take an easy fight, so that's why I took Damian. He's a big guy. But we've got to take risks. I've still got it in me, man. I've just got to stay active and I want to fight again." Knyba improved his professional record to 18 wins and one defeat with the victory.
